articles.title: Bunting Scallop
articles.summary: Rows of nested arc scallops like bunting swags, repeated in stacked bands across the surface A scribbly web of pale arcs and spokes, busy where fans pile up and empty in gaps; it reads as a loose white and pink line tangle, not as flags or bunting.
articles.what: Scattered swags of patriotic bunting — nested red/white/blue arc scallops flung at random rotations like festival bunting draped every which way Up close: Thin hairline fans: each is a quarter-to-half arc with straight spokes radiating from a hub, like folding hand fans or bicycle wheels cut in half. Fans overlap at random angles in pale white-grey and dusty red; no blue shows. Lines are one to three pixels wide. From a distance: A scribbly web of pale arcs and spokes, busy where fans pile up and empty in gaps; it reads as a loose white and pink line tangle, not as flags or bunting. Group: Let Freedom Ring. Texture detail: medium.
how: Click a zone card and open the PATTERN section.
Click Pattern 1 on this Layer to open the picker.
Open the group "Let Freedom Ring" or search for "Bunting Scallop", then click it.
Drag Scale below 1.00 until the repeats look fine on the car.
Switch Paint mode to Blend if you want to keep your paint colour.
tips: Hood, roof and doors: wide panels have room for the fans to overlap
Quarter panels as a background texture; avoid small trim where one fan is bigger than the part
Hairlines leave numbers mostly clear, but a pile-up of white spokes can cross a number; use solid bold numbers with an outline.
Dark
Pairs well with: gloss white, satin navy, matte red, chrome.
pitfalls: Not bunting flags: the lines are open fans with spokes, no filled triangles or solid stripes
Not scallop scale armour: scallops here are thin outlines, not packed rows
Avoid: too busy on complex bases, avoid on dark matte.
articles.intent_note: Pattern-design shelf: the structure of the pattern matters, not the colour it is printed in.
articles.paint_advice: Pattern contrast 91 out of 100: strong, it shows over almost any plain colour. It covers about 29 percent of the tile, so a lot of base colour stays visible. Use Paint mode Blend to keep your colour; Overlay prints the pattern's own colours over it.
